summary: This standards-track document modifies the distance-vector routing approach used by RIP so that updates are sent only when something changes, rather than on a constant timer. That matters for demand circuits such as dial-up links, where periodic chatter would keep an expensive connection open for no reason.

eli5.summary: Instead of calling your friend every minute to say nothing changed, you only call when there is news.

subtitle: RIP that speaks only when something changes, so dial-up and other on-demand links can hang up between calls.

tldr.problem: Periodic RIP and SAP broadcasts every 30 or 60 seconds keep on-demand WAN circuits such as X.25 and ISDN from closing, and add load even on fixed links.
tldr.mechanism: Triggered RIP sends routing updates only when asked or when the database or circuit state changes, and adds three packet types (Update Request, Update Response, Update Acknowledge) with sequence numbers and retransmission for reliability.
tldr.outcome: Routes learned over the WAN are kept as permanent until a flush or a circuit failure, while LAN behavior stays unchanged, so it interoperates with plain RIP implementations.

today: RFC 2091 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its abstract presents it as an improvement over the Demand RIP proposal.

sections.title: The Demand Circuit Problem
sections.content:
Routers on connection oriented networks, such as X.25 and ISDN, open circuits on demand and give them up when traffic subsides. Periodic broadcasting by distance vector protocols (IP RIP, IP RIP V2, Netware RIP and SAP) generally prevents those circuits from closing. Even on fixed point-to-point links, the overhead of RIP, and more so SAP, every 30 or 60 seconds can interrupt normal data transfer.

This document modifies the protocols to send information on the WAN only when the routing database is updated or the circuit manager reports a change in reachability of a next hop router. Datagrams are not guaranteed to get through, so an acknowledgement and retransmission system is added. On LANs the protocols run unmodified, so they interoperate with implementations of the original specifications.

The abstract says this has efficiency advantages over the earlier Demand RIP proposal: after the initial exchange only changed information is sent, the receiver can apply changes immediately, and there is no limit of 255 fragments because it uses no fragmentation.
sections.eli5: A phone line that is always busy with chit-chat can never hang up. This lets routers talk only when they have news, so the line can rest.

sections.title: How Triggered Updates Work
sections.content:
A circuit manager sits between the connectionless network layers (IP and IPX) and the connection oriented WAN. It opens a virtual circuit to the next hop router when there is data to send and closes it when traffic stops. If it cannot get a circuit, it tells the routing application the destination is unreachable (circuit down), and later reports circuit up when recovery succeeds.

Routing updates are transmitted on the WAN only in four cases: a specific request arrives; the database is changed by information from another interface; the circuit manager reports a change from circuit down to circuit up; or the unit is first powered on, which counts as circuit down to up and may carry no routes. In the first, third and fourth cases the full database is sent. In the second only the latest changes are sent.

Requests and responses both need acknowledgement, and are retransmitted if none arrives.
sections.eli5: A helper watches the phone line. It tells the router when a neighbor can be reached and when not, and the router speaks up only when it must.

sections.title: The Routing Database Rules
sections.content:
Entries learned from broadcasts on LANs are temporary and expire unless refreshed. Entries learned from a triggered response on the WAN are permanent: they must not time out in the normal course of events. Once an update arrives from a next hop router on the WAN, its entries are presumed reachable unless proven otherwise. On circuit down, entries are marked temporary and aged (some implementations may skip this), then marked unreachable for a hold down period of 120 seconds. On circuit up, the routers exchange messages to refresh their databases. Too many unacknowledged retransmissions can also mark a next hop unreachable.

No routing information may be lost or discarded, so all alternative routes should be retained. Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse must be used, and a route is poisoned only if it is the best route. Poison Reverse is needed because a router may advertise a route to its partner and later learn a better route from that partner; without it the partner would not know to discard the inferior route.

The database is treated as a sequence ordered by last update time. A change to the best route gives it a new highest sequence number. Updates run from the oldest entry to the newest, and an entry that was sent and acknowledged is generally never resent.
sections.eli5: News that came over the expensive line is kept until someone says to forget it, instead of fading away on a timer. Old and new news are kept in order, so only the new news gets sent.

sections.title: New Packet Types and the Update Header
sections.content:
Three packet types must be supported. For IP RIP version 1 and version 2 they are identified by the Command field, and for Netware RIP and SAP by the Operation field, using the same values: 9 Update Request, 10 Update Response and 11 Update Acknowledge. Each adds a 4-octet Update header.

An Update Request asks the peer for all appropriate routes. It is retransmitted every 5 seconds until an Update Response with the Flush flag set arrives, and is sent at power on and on a circuit down to up change. An Update Response carries zero or more routes and is retransmitted until acknowledged. It must be sent with the Flush flag set in response to a request, at power on (without routes, to flush the peer's table from a previous incarnation) and after circuit down to up. The rest of the database follows as responses without Flush. An Update Acknowledge is sent for every Update Response and echoes the Flush flag.

The header has a Version (must be 1; other versions are silently discarded), a Flush byte and a 2-byte Sequence Number. The sequence number is incremented for each new Update Response, unchanged on retransmission, and wraps at 65535. It has meaning only to the sender. The peer returns the same sequence number and Flush value in its acknowledgement.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of notes: please tell me everything, here is some news, and got it. Each news note has a number so the sender knows which one was received.

sections.title: Timers and Retransmission
sections.content:
When an Update Response with the Flush flag set is received, all routes learned from that next hop start timing out as if learned from a conventional response: the database timer (usually 180 seconds) runs and then the route is advertised as unreachable while a hold down timer of 120 seconds runs. The hold down timer also starts on a circuit down message or when a reachable route becomes unreachable in an incoming response. A route may be deleted when it expires only if its unreachability has been propagated to all WAN destinations or the remaining ones are circuit down.

The retransmission timer resends Update Requests until a Flush arrives and Update Responses until an acknowledgement with the same sequence number arrives. With call setup time on the order of a second, 5 seconds is suggested. A limit on retransmissions should be set, for example 180 seconds; after that routes via the next hop are marked unreachable and the router may poll at a reduced frequency, such as minutes.

With several packets in flight, a retransmission must be rebuilt from the database so it contains only routes that still apply, and the datalink must not reorder datagrams. The RFC advises having only one packet in flight for simplicity. An optional over-subscription timer delays marking routes unreachable when there are more next hops than channels, for example 3 next hops on an ISDN BRI that supports 2 calls.
sections.eli5: If a note is not confirmed within a few seconds, the sender sends it again, but only the parts that are still true. If the neighbor stays silent for a long time, the sender assumes it is gone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The circuit manager is given a list of physical addresses so it can call the next hop router, and should accept incoming calls only from that same list. The routing or service advertising task must be given a list of logical addresses to which triggered updates are sent; this may be a subset of the circuit manager's list. The RFC adds that RIP Version 2 also allows further authentication of Triggered RIP packets.
sections.eli5: A router should only call, and only answer calls from, neighbors on its list of known friends.

items.label: Update Request
items.desc: Asks the peer for all appropriate routes.

items.label: Update Response
items.desc: Carries zero or more routes; retransmitted until acknowledged.

items.label: Update Acknowledge
items.desc: Sent for every Update Response, echoing sequence number and Flush.
